title: Joy and reward: expecting something good and getting it
description: A sign that something good is coming, the wait, the moment it arrives, and the enjoyment of it. This is the best-mapped positive state in brain research, mostly because it can be produced in a scanner by letting people win small amounts of money. It is an ordinary state, not a condition, so there is no "typical response" to compare it with.
caveat: Most of this comes from one kind of experiment: people in a scanner see a cue, wait, and then win or do not win money, food or other rewards. That is a narrow slice of what people mean by joy. The split into wanting and enjoying comes from researchers who argue that the two rely on different brain mechanisms; the evidence for where enjoyment itself is generated is mainly from animals. None of the regions shown is a "pleasure centre": the same striatal, thalamic and amygdala regions also respond when people expect a loss, and a large pooled analysis of positive and negative feeling found that the same limbic regions serve both.

phases.name: A promise
phases.caption: A sign that something good may be on its way. Dopamine neurons in the midbrain, which respond to reward-related signals, send their output up to the striatum.

phases.name: Looking forward
phases.caption: The wait. A group of deep regions is active together: the striatum, including the nucleus accumbens, the thalamus and the amygdala. This is wanting, not yet enjoying.

citations.authors: Oldham S, Murawski C, Fornito A, Youssef G, Yücel M, Lorenzetti V
citations.title: The anticipation and outcome phases of reward and loss processing: A neuroimaging meta-analysis of the monetary incentive delay task.
citations.quote: The result of reward anticipation (contrast RA) revealed a large cluster of brain regions around the striatal‐thalamic regions of the brain, encompassing the ventral, including the nucleus accumbens (NAcc), and the dorsal striatum, extending to the bilateral amygdala

phases.name: It arrives
phases.caption: The good thing happens. The ventral striatum responds again, now joined by the orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, which track how much something is worth, and the posterior cingulate.

citations.title: The anticipation and outcome phases of reward and loss processing: A neuroimaging meta-analysis of the monetary incentive delay task.
citations.quote: the contrast of reward outcome (contrast RO) showed a large cluster in the ventral striatum which extended into the subcallosal, followed by another large cluster in the OFC/vmPFC, and a smaller clusters in the dorsal PCC and amygdala cortex

phases.name: Enjoying it
phases.caption: The pleasure itself. In people, activity in the orbitofrontal cortex goes with how pleasant something feels. Where pleasure is generated is known mainly from animals, and it is not the dopamine system: dopamine drives wanting more than enjoying.

order.rationale: Scanner studies separate the wait from the outcome but not the outcome from the enjoyment that follows. Showing enjoyment as its own later step is an inference from the argument that wanting and enjoying are different processes.

regions.explanation: The midbrain source of the dopamine neurons that run up to the nucleus accumbens. This system is activated by reward-related signals. It was long described as the brain's pleasure system, but the researchers cited here argue that dopamine is needed for wanting a reward, not for enjoying it.

regions.explanation: The ventral striatum, active both while people wait for a reward and when it arrives. This is the most consistent finding in reward research. It is not specific to good things: a similar cluster responds when people expect a loss. In animals, activity here also tracks how much a taste is liked.
